section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Logic of Base-3
section_1.content: Introduce the ternary system (0, 1, 2) as the natural language of branching structures. Contrast with binary to show why ternary fits structures with three-way choices.
section_1.example: A smart robot moving between three charging stations (A, B, C) where each step is represented by a digit (0, 1, or 2).

section_2.title: The Constrained Towers of Hanoi
section_2.content: Explain the variation where disks can only move between adjacent pegs (A↔B, B↔C). Reveal that the sequence of moves to solve this follows the ternary counting pattern.
section_2.example: Representing disk movements as a sequence: 0 for A→B, 1 for B→C, 2 for A→C (an illegal jump). We show that the 'legal' path avoids digit 2, forming a self-similar path.

section_3.title: Visualizing the Sierpinski Triangle
section_3.content: Connect the Hanoi state space to the Sierpinski Triangle. As the number of disks increases, the state diagram converges to the Sierpinski gasket, illustrating how recursive movement forms fractal geometry.
section_3.example: An animation showing a 'path-finding ant' traversing the edges of a Sierpinski triangle; each turn at a vertex corresponds to adding a digit in a ternary expansion.

section_4.title: Synthesis: The Fractal Geometry of Computation
section_4.content: Summarize the isomorphism: The set of legal moves in the constrained Hanoi problem is the graph of the Sierpinski triangle. Ternary counting serves as the coordinate system for this infinite fractal space.
section_4.example: A visual overlay showing a 3-disk Hanoi state diagram perfectly mapping onto the 3rd iteration of a Sierpinski triangle, using colors to track the 'ternary address' of each position.
